conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having some vision changes and a headache today. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, around 10 this morning, I suddenly lost vision in the left side of my left eye—like from 10 o’clock down. Then everything looked wavy. Shortly after, I got a throbbing headache on the right side and top of my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did you feel nauseous or sensitive to light or sound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very sensitive to light and noise, and I felt nauseous. I also had a brief sharp pain in my left eye. I haven’t had a migraine like this since menopause—before that, they were on the right side but never with vision changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned in the ER that you used to respond to a triptan injection. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a subcutaneous sumatriptan used to help. But I haven’t needed it in years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your labs. Your sodium is a bit low and potassium is high, which can happen with your Addison’s disease. We’re giving you IV fluids and a higher dose of prednisone to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I was in for something similar—my potassium was high then too. Is this another Addison’s flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks that way. The low sodium and high potassium support that. We’ve started you on 10 mg of prednisone twice daily—double your usual dose—for stress coverage. We also gave kayexalate to help lower your potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay on that higher dose long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just for two more days. Then you’ll go back to your regular 5 mg. Your levels are already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your head CT came back normal—no bleeding, stroke, or mass. The neurologist and eye doctor both agree your symptoms are consistent with a migraine with aura.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the vision changes were part of the migraine? I was really worried it was a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the visual symptoms—like the blind spot and wavy lines—are classic for migraine aura. They can happen even if you haven’t had migraines in years. Your exam was normal, and the CT supports this isn’t a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My headache is much better now. What about the potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was 5.6 when you arrived, but it’s now down to 5.0, which is safe. It improved with fluids and kayexalate. We’ll check it again as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re ready to send you home. We’ll give you sumatriptan injections for future migraines and ketorolac for pain. Keep taking the 10 mg prednisone twice daily for two more days, then return to your usual dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my potassium goes up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with a dose of kayexalate to use only if your potassium is high and you feel unwell, but your levels should stabilize as your Addison’s is better controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please follow up with your primary doctor to review the final CT report and your labs. Also schedule an outpatient MRI to further rule out other causes, even though we’re confident this was a migraine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my clonazepam? I’ve been using it for anxiety and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your usual dose of clonazepam as needed. We’ve also adjusted your trazodone for sleep. Everything else, like your thyroid and fludrocortisone, stays the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better knowing it wasn’t something more serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest today, avoid triggers like bright lights, and reach out if the headache returns or you feel off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to come back if I use the sumatriptan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, just use it as directed—one injection, and repeat in an hour if needed. But if symptoms are different or worsen, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.
